stem: How many votes does each member usually have at a co-operative's general meeting?

options.content: One vote, whatever the number of shares
One vote for each share owned
options.rationale: That is how a company works.

options.content: Votes in proportion to produce delivered
options.rationale: Trade affects the refund, not votes.

options.content: Only committee members may vote

explanation: Democratic control: one member, one vote.

stem: A co-operative that buys fertiliser and seed in bulk and sells them to its members is a:

options.content: supply co-operative
marketing co-operative
savings and credit co-operative
producer co-operative

explanation: Supply (input) co-operatives buy inputs in bulk for members.

stem: How is the surplus of a co-operative usually returned to members?

options.content: Equally to every member, whatever their trade with it
Mainly in proportion to shares held
Only to the committee members
In proportion to each member's trade with it

explanation: The surplus is returned according to use of the co-operative, such as litres delivered.

stem: What is the main purpose of a co-operative's by-laws?

options.content: To list the prices of all members' produce
options.rationale: Prices are not set in by-laws.

options.content: To record the daily milk deliveries
To advertise the co-operative's goods
To set out its rules and how it is run

explanation: By-laws set the name, aims, membership, shares, elections, meetings and sharing of surplus.

stem: Smallholders want loans for inputs but banks refuse them. Which type of co-operative would help most?

options.content: A marketing co-operative only
options.rationale: Markets produce but may not lend.

options.content: A producer co-operative only
A consumer co-operative
A savings and credit co-operative

explanation: SACCOs pool members' savings and lend to members at fair interest.
hints: Which type handles savings and loans?

stem: Why does registration with the registrar of co-operatives help a co-operative?

options.content: It guarantees that the co-operative will make a surplus every year
It gives the group legal status to own property and borrow
It allows the government to run it
It removes the need to keep accounts
options.rationale: Accounts must still be kept and audited.

explanation: Registration makes the co-operative a legal body that can own property, open accounts, borrow and sign contracts.
hints: What can a registered body do in its own name?

stem: Members of a marketing co-operative often sell to roadside traders who pay cash, instead of delivering to the co-operative. What is the most serious effect?

options.content: The members will get larger patronage refunds
It cannot meet contracts or recover input loans
The co-operative's costs per tonne will fall
options.rationale: Fixed costs are spread over less produce, so they rise.

options.content: Buyers will offer the co-operative higher prices

explanation: Without members' produce the co-operative loses contracts, cannot recover loans and its costs per unit rise.
hints: What does the co-operative depend on?

stem: Which is a principle of co-operatives?

options.content: Profit shared only by the largest shareholders
Control by an outside company
Voluntary and open membership
Membership limited to one family

explanation: Anyone able to use the services and accept the duties may join.

stem: In a co-operative a member who owns many shares has more votes than a member who owns one share.
explanation: False. Each member has one vote regardless of shares.

stem: Match each type of co-operative with what it does.

right.content: Members farm together with shared resources
Buys inputs in bulk for members

explanation: Know the function of each type.

payload.template: The meeting held every year at which members receive the accounts and elect the committee is the {{blank:a}} general meeting.

stem: Give the term for the money left after a co-operative has paid all its costs for the year.
Assume fertiliser costs US\$38 a bag in town. A co-operative buys it at US\$33 a bag plus US\$1.50 a bag transport. Calculate a member's saving on 25 bags.
explanation: Co-operative cost = 33 + 1.50 = US\$34.50; saving per bag = US\$3.50; × 25 = US\$87.50. Forgetting transport gives US\$125.
workedSolution: 1. Co-operative cost = 33 + 1.50 = US\$34.50; saving per bag = US\$3.50; × 25 = US\$87.50. Forgetting transport gives US\$125.
hints: Saving per bag = town price − (co-operative price + transport).

stem: A dairy co-operative returns US\$6,000 of its surplus to members in proportion to milk delivered. Members delivered 150,000 L in the year; Thandeka delivered 3,600 L. Calculate Thandeka's refund.
workedSolution:
1. Refund per litre = 6,000 ÷ 150,000 = US\$0.04.
2. Thandeka's refund = 3,600 × 0.04 = US\$144.
hints: Refund per litre = amount shared ÷ total litres.

stem: A new co-operative has 45 members, each buying 4 shares at US\$10 a share. Calculate the share capital raised.
Explain **two** benefits a smallholder gains from joining a marketing co-operative.

points.description: Produce from many members is assembled into large lots.
Giving bargaining power for better prices / attracting large buyers and contracts.
Shared facilities such as storage, cooling, grading and transport.
Which a single smallholder could not afford, reducing losses and costs; surplus returned to members.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The co-operative combines members' produce into large lots, so it can bargain for better prices and win contracts with big buyers. It also provides shared storage, cooling and transport that one smallholder could not afford, reducing losses and costs.

hints: Think of bargaining power and shared facilities.

stem: Suggest **two** problems a farmers' co-operative may face and a solution to each.

points.description: Problem 1, e.g. poor management or dishonest officials / misuse of funds.
Solution: train the committee and staff, keep audited accounts and present them to members at the AGM.
Problem 2, e.g. lack of capital / late payment / side-selling by members.
Solution: build reserves and members' shares, seek credit as a registered body / pay members promptly / enforce by-laws fairly.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Officials may lack business skills or misuse funds; training and audited accounts presented at the AGM help. Members may side-sell when traders pay cash; prompt payment by the co-operative and fair enforcement of the by-laws keep them loyal.

stem:
A multipurpose co-operative near Gokwe had these results for one year (assumed figures). Members delivered 350 t of maize.

| Item | US\$ |
| --- | --- |
| Income: Sales of members' maize | 96,000 |
| Income: Sales of inputs to members | 41,000 |
| Expense: Payments to members for maize | 82,000 |
| Expense: Cost of inputs bought | 36,000 |
| Expense: Transport and storage | 7,400 |
| Expense: Wages | 4,800 |
| Expense: Other running costs | 1,800 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the surplus for the year.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: The AGM puts 30% of the surplus into reserves. Calculate the amount left to return to members.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The amount for members is shared in proportion to maize delivered. Farai delivered 12 t. Calculate his refund.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State **one** reason for keeping part of the surplus as a reserve.

points.description: To buy or repair equipment / meet future losses or emergencies / expand services without borrowing.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why the surplus is shared by maize delivered rather than by shares held.

points.description: Co-operative principle: the surplus comes from members' trade with the co-operative, so it is returned to those who used it most.
This rewards loyal members who deliver their crop (discouraging side-selling); interest on shares is limited so investors do not take control.

explanation: Calculate a co-operative's surplus and patronage refunds and explain the principle.
hints: Refund per tonne = amount for members ÷ tonnes delivered.

stem: Thirty goat keepers near Masvingo want to sell their goats together to a buyer in Bulawayo and to buy dip chemicals and dewormers in bulk. An extension officer advises them to form a co-operative.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which type of co-operative best suits their aims?

options.content: Savings and credit co-operative
options.rationale: They have not asked for loans.

options.content: Producer co-operative
options.rationale: They keep their own goats; they do not farm jointly.

options.content: Multipurpose co-operative
Consumer co-operative

parts.explanation: They want both marketing (selling goats) and supply (buying chemicals): a multipurpose co-operative.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe **three** steps the goat keepers should follow to form and register the co-operative.

points.description: Hold a first (inaugural) meeting, agree to form the co-operative and elect an interim committee.
Study whether the business is viable and draw up by-laws (rules on membership, shares, committee, sharing surplus).
Apply to the registrar of co-operatives for registration, sell shares and hold the first AGM to elect the management committee.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how selling the goats together could raise their income.

points.description: A large lot of goats attracts a big buyer and gives bargaining power for a better price.
Transport and selling costs are shared, so cost per goat falls (higher net price).

explanation: Choose a type of co-operative, describe its formation and explain a benefit.
hints: Think of the steps from idea to registration.
